passage: Tiny notebook, blue cover. That's the whole secret, Jatin. For one month I wrote down everything I bought, even the five-rupee stuff, and I did not judge myself. On the last day I added it up and my stomach dropped: chips, sweets and phone recharges together were about a third of my money. I had no idea. I always thought it was clothes, or that one birthday gift. Nobody told me to stop. I just looked at the page and decided, this is a lot for chips and data I barely use. So I made two changes: treats only on Fridays, and a smaller recharge plan. I didn't cut everything, because I like a samosa. I'm Usha, the only girl in class with a ledger, and Mum calls me her little accountant. I'm still eating samosas.

passage:
I'm Neelam. Payal and I share a desk, and for the whole of July she carried a tiny notebook in her pencil box. Every time she bought anything, she wrote it down: date, what, how much. Samosa, 15. Pen, 10. Recharge, 49. Chips, 20. It seemed a bit much to me.
On the first of August she showed me the totals, grouped by type. Snacks and phone top-ups together were a third of everything she had spent. She looked honestly surprised.
She didn't do anything dramatic. She said she'd keep one canteen snack on Fridays and bring fruit from home on other days, and she switched to a cheaper recharge pack her brother told her about. She still bought stickers when she wanted them.
By the end of August her notebook had a new line at the bottom: saved. I don't know exactly how much. But she was smiling when she wrote it.

qa.q: How much did a recharge cost in Payal's notebook?
How did Payal feel on seeing the totals on the first of August?
qa.a: Payal looked honestly surprised to see that snacks and top-ups took a third of her spending.

qa.q: Why did trimming only snacks and top-ups work better than cutting everything?
qa.a: It targeted the two biggest leaks while leaving room for small joys like stickers, so the change was easy to keep.

qa.q: How does Payal's month look to Neelam?
qa.a: Neelam first thought the notebook was a bit much, then saw it lead to a real, cheerful change.

passage:
1 March: Seema can't work out where her monthly pocket money goes. She's always broke by the twentieth. Her cousin Dolma suggests writing down every single purchase for a month.
Mid-March, a Saturday: The notebook is filling up. Momos with friends, 40. Recharge, 99. Cold drink, 20. Another recharge, 49, because the data ran out. Seema is annoyed at how often “momos” and “recharge” appear.
31 March: She adds it all up on the back page and circles two numbers. Food outside and phone top-ups together come to about a third of everything she spent. She decides, because she wants to and not because anyone told her, to have momos only on Saturdays and to switch to a monthly data pack instead of small top-ups.
30 April: For the first time, she still has money left on the thirtieth.

qa.a: Writing down every single purchase for a month.

qa.q: How did Seema feel seeing "momos" and "recharge" so often?
qa.a: Seema felt annoyed with herself as the pattern became obvious.

qa.q: What else could Seema do now that April went well?
qa.a: Keep tracking for another month to check the change holds, and ask a parent where best to keep what's left.

qa.q: How might Dolma see Seema's April result?
qa.a: Dolma is probably pleased the simple suggestion worked and that Seema made her own choices about what to cut.

grounding: Shows a teen recording every purchase for a month, finding snacks and top-ups take about a third, and trimming those two areas by her own choice.
